**Subject:** Non‑payment of Full‑and‑Final Settlement – What you can do legally --- ### 1. What the law says about a full‑and‑final (F&F) settlement | Statute / Rule | What it covers | Relevant provisions | |----------------|----------------|----------------------| | **Payment of Wages Act, 1936** (as amended) | Payment of wages, salary, arrears, gratuity, leave encashment, etc. | Sec. 15 – “Wages shall be paid … within the stipulated time”. The Act applies to any employee drawing a wage of **Rs 10,000 per month or more** (the threshold was raised to Rs 10,000 in 2020). A marketing manager in a private firm will fall within its ambit. | | **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947** (IDA) – Section 2(oo) “termination of service” & Section 10(1) “settlement of disputes” | When an employee is terminated (including resignation) the employer must pay all dues within **30 days** of the termination date. Failure to do so is a “contempt of the authority” and a “unfair labour practice”. | | **The Maharashtra Shops and Establishments (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 2017** (MSE Act) | Governs private sector establishments in Mumbai. Section 13(1) requires that **all wages, allowances, gratuity, leave encashment, etc., be paid on or before the last day of employment**. | | **The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972** (if you have ≥5 years service) | Gratuity must be paid within **30 days** of the date it becomes payable. | | **The Income Tax Act, 1961** – Section 192 & 194C (TDS on settlement) | The employer must deduct TDS on any settlement amount (if applicable) and issue a Form 16/16A. Non‑deduction does not excuse non‑payment. | | **Contract Law – Indian Contract Act, 1872** | The employment contract (or the resignation letter together with the company’s F&F policy) creates a **contractual obligation** to pay the agreed settlement. Non‑performance is a breach of contract. | > **Bottom line:** Under the **MSE Act** and the **Payment of Wages Act**, the employer **must** clear all dues **within 30 days** of the employee’s last working day. Your last working day was **14 August 2026**; therefore the employer should have paid the settlement **by 13 September 2026**. As of today (5 Nov 2026) the payment is overdue. --- ### 2. Immediate steps you should take | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **2.1. Send a formal legal notice** | Draft a **demand notice** on a lawyer’s letterhead, stating:
• Your employment details (designation, dates of service).
• Amount due (Rs 1,35,000) and a breakdown (salary, leave encashment, gratuity, etc.).
• Reference to **MSE Act, Sec. 13(1)** and **Payment of Wages Act, Sec. 15**.
• Demand payment **within 7 days** of receipt of the notice, failing which you will initiate legal/compliance proceedings. | A statutory notice is a prerequisite for filing a complaint before the Labour Commissioner under the IDA and also shows the employer that you are serious. | | **2.2. File a complaint with the Labour Commissioner (Maharashtra)** | Use **Form‑L** (Complaint under the Industrial Disputes Act) and submit it to the **Maharashtra Labour Commissioner, Mumbai**. Attach:
• Copy of resignation letter (dated 14 Aug 2026).
• Salary slips, F&F policy, email trail with HR.
• The demand notice you sent. | The Labour Commissioner can **issue a “show‑cause notice”** to the employer and can pass an **interim award** ordering payment of the dues, with interest at **8 % per annum** (as per *M/s. R. K. Industries Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra*, 2009). | | **2.3. Approach the appropriate Court** | If the employer does not comply with the Labour Commissioner’s award, you may file a **civil suit for recovery of money** under **Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act** (damages for breach of contract) in the **Mumbai Civil Court (Maharashtra)**. You can also claim **interest under Section 34 of the Negotiable Instruments Act** (if you treat the settlement as a “promissory note”). | A civil suit is a fallback if the labour‑commissioner route stalls or if the employer contests the award. | | **2.4. File a criminal complaint for “cheating”** (optional) | If the employer deliberately refuses to pay after promising settlement, you may lodge an FIR under **Section 420 IPC** (cheating) and **Section 201 IPC** (causing loss of property). | This is rarely used for pure wage disputes but can add pressure, especially if the employer is a corporate entity with a known pattern of non‑payment. | | **2.5. Preserve evidence** | Keep:
• All email correspondence (including the HR’s last reply on 1 Oct 2026).
• Screenshots of the company’s F&F policy (usually on the intranet).
• Pay‑slips, bank statements showing no credit of Rs 1,35,000.
• Witness statements from colleagues who can confirm your last working day and the settlement promise. | Evidence is crucial for the Labour Commissioner and the court. | --- ### 3. Interest and penalties you can claim | Provision | Rate / Method | |-----------|---------------| | **Interest on delayed wages** – *Payment of Wages Act* | **8 % per annum** from the date the wages became payable (i.e., 15 Aug 2026) until actual payment. | | **Interest under the IDA** – *Section 23(2)* | Same 8 % per annum, compounded annually. | | **Penalty under MSE Act** – *Section 13(2)* | The employer may be liable to pay **double the amount** of wages if the delay exceeds **30 days** (as per *Maharashtra State Board of Secondary Education v. Smt. Shakuntala*, 2015). | | **Legal costs** – *Civil Procedure Code* | The court may order the employer to pay your attorney’s fees and court costs. | --- ### 4. Sample wording of the demand notice (to be sent by a lawyer) > **[Law Firm Letterhead]** > **Date:** 5 Nov 2026 > **To:** Human Resources Department, [Company Name], [Company Address], Mumbai. > **Subject:** **Demand for Payment of Full‑and‑Final Settlement – Rs 1,35,000** > > Dear Sir/Madam, > > 1. I was employed as **Marketing Manager** with your company from **[date of joining]** to **14 August 2026**. I tendered my resignation on **[date of resignation]** and my last working day was **14 August 2026**. > 2. As per the company’s Full‑and‑Final Settlement policy (circulated on **[date]**) and the terms of my employment, the following amounts were due to me: > - Salary (incl. arrears) – Rs _____ > - Leave encashment – Rs _____ > - Gratuity (if applicable) – Rs _____ > - Other allowances – Rs _____ > **Total: Rs 1,35,000**. > 3. Under **Section 13(1) of the Maharashtra Shops & Establishments Act, 2017**, **Section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936**, and **Section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947**, the employer is obligated to pay all dues **within 30 days** of termination. The statutory deadline expired on **13 September 2026**. > 4. Despite repeated reminders (e‑mail dated 1 Oct 2026, 5 Oct 2026, etc.), no payment has been made. > 5. Accordingly, you are hereby **required to pay the full amount of Rs 1,35,000 together with statutory interest at 8 % per annum** within **seven (7) days** of receipt of this notice. > 6. Failure to comply will compel me to: > a) File a complaint before the **Maharashtra Labour Commissioner** under the **Industrial Disputes Act**; > b) Initiate a **civil suit for recovery of money** with interest and costs; and > c) Pursue appropriate **criminal proceedings** for cheating. > > Please treat this matter with urgency. > > **Yours faithfully,** > _______________________ > **[Your Name]** > **[Your Contact Details]** --- ### 5. Timeline you can realistically expect | Timeframe | Activity | |-----------|----------| | **0–7 days** | Send the legal notice (step 2.1). | | **7–30 days** | If no response, file complaint with Labour Commissioner (step 2.2). | | **30–60 days** | Labour Commissioner issues show‑cause notice; employer may settle voluntarily. | | **60–90 days** | If employer still refuses, the Commissioner passes an **interim award** ordering payment with interest. | | **90–180 days** | If the employer does not comply with the award, you can file a **civil execution petition** to attach bank accounts or property. | | **Beyond 180 days** | If the employer is a corporate entity, you may also approach the **National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)** for a winding‑up petition for non‑payment of dues (rare, but an option if the company is insolvent). | --- ### 6. Practical tips & precautions 1. **Do not sign any “settlement waiver”** that the HR may try to get you to sign now; it could be used to bar future claims. 2. **Maintain a polite but firm tone** in all communications; avoid any language that could be construed as harassment. 3. **If you have a service agreement or an employee handbook**, attach those as annexures to the notice – they strengthen the contractual claim. 4. **Consider mediation**: The Labour Commissioner’s office often offers a **conciliation** stage. If the employer is willing, a mediated settlement (with a written receipt) can save time and costs. 5. **Keep copies of everything** (originals and digital). Use **registered post (with acknowledgment due)** for the notice, and keep the receipt as proof of service. --- ### 7. Bottom line for you - **Your employer is legally bound** to pay the Rs 1,35,000 (plus interest) **within 30 days** of your last working day. - **You have a clear statutory remedy** under the **Maharashtra Shops & Establishments Act** and the **Payment of Wages Act**. - **Start with a formal demand notice** (preferably through a lawyer) and, if ignored, **approach the Maharashtra Labour Commissioner**. - **Interest of 8 % per annum** and possibly **double wages** as penalty can be claimed, making the amount recoverable higher than the original Rs 1,35,000. If you need a draft notice or assistance in filing the complaint, please let me know and I can connect you with a labour‑law specialist in Mumbai. --- **Disclaimer:** This answer is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal representation. For personalized advice, please consult a qualified advocate who can review all documents and facts in detail.
